Apoptosis dismantles a cell through regulated pathways. In the intrinsic pathway, internal stress affects mitochondrial membranes; cytochrome c can then help assemble an apoptosome that activates caspase-9 and executioner caspases. In the extrinsic pathway, signals detected by cell-surface receptors can activate caspase-8 and the execution machinery. Some cells require mitochondrial amplification of the extrinsic signal. Death-receptor stimulation can instead promote survival or inflammation, so receptor binding alone does not prove that apoptosis will occur. Apoptosis and clearance are not always immunologically silent.

The intrinsic pathway responds to internal stress, including DNA damage, growth-factor withdrawal, endoplasmic-reticulum stress and oxidative stress. A central event is mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization (MOMP). BCL2-family proteins regulate this event; BAX and BAK are important pore-forming effectors in the conventional pathway. Released cytochrome c associates with APAF1 and pro-caspase-9 to form the apoptosome. Activated caspase-9 activates executioner caspases-3 and -7. Released SMAC can counter inhibitors of apoptosis. The pathway is more complex than a single irreversible switch: the source also discusses possible BAX/BAK-independent mechanisms whose pathophysiological relevance remains uncertain. Apoptotic cells initially retain plasma-membrane integrity, allowing phagocytic clearance. Apoptosis is not invariably immunologically silent; uncleared cells in culture can progress to secondary necrosis.

Caspase-8 then connects receptor signalling to executioner caspases. In type I cells, executioner activation can be sufficient; in type II cells, cleavage of BID links the signal to mitochondrial BAX/BAK-dependent permeabilization and caspase-9 activation. Caspase-10 contributions vary between species and remain debated; rodents lack a functional Casp10 gene. These qualifications matter when extrapolating experimental pathways to human disease.

Oral epithelium is the stratified squamous tissue covering the oral mucosa. Its main cells are keratinocytes; minority populations include melanocytes, Langerhans cells, Merkel cells, and transient inflammatory cells.

In keratinized oral regions, the layers are basal, spinous, granular, and an outer cornified layer. In nonkeratinized oral regions, they are basal, spinous, intermediate, and superficial layers. The source describes cornified surfaces that resist mastication and nonkeratinized lining that can stretch.

Proliferation occurs in the basal layer; new cells differentiate and move upward. The source reports epithelial renewal over 5–40 days depending on the region, so this is not a uniform turnover rate for the whole mouth. This renewal relates to epithelial stem cells in the basal layer. Cancer progressively disrupts the ordered architecture and balanced renewal described for normal oral mucosa.

Necrosis describes a cell-death phenotype in which plasma-membrane integrity is lost and cell contents escape. It can follow passive injury or regulated cell-death programmes. Thus, necrosis is not synonymous with an exclusively unregulated mechanism. Lytic release of intracellular damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) can trigger inflammation. Different necrotic programmes and passive damage do not necessarily have identical immunogenic effects. This membrane-based explanation does not by itself establish a complete microscopic subtype, mechanism or personal diagnosis.

Apoptosis is not invariably non-inflammatory. Although it is commonly described as a non-inflammatory process, release of particular damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) can make apoptotic cell death immunogenic. Secondary necrosis can contribute to this release, but it does not explain all DAMP release: some DAMPs are preferentially released by apoptotic rather than necrotic cells. An intact-versus-ruptured membrane distinction therefore does not by itself settle immunogenicity. These are source-era mechanistic observations, not a diagnosis or a universal prediction of tissue inflammation.
